sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Cáishén** (*caishen*) — Wealth, Prosperity, New Year · God of wealth — belongs to the Chinese tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Wealth, Prosperity, New Year". The name means "God of wealth"[^1].

**Cáishén** belongs to the Chinese tradition, where it is associated with wealth, prosperity, new year.[^2]

PuniCodex restores the name as **Cáishén** and serves its temple at [caishen.com](https://punicodex.com/caishen/). The restoration preserves at least one distinctive feature — a diacritic or a distinctive letter — that the ASCII form loses, and exactly one historically valid Unicode restoration exists, which places the name in Tier 1. The plain ASCII form *caishen* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete[^2].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The name is attested in Chinese characters as **財神**. Etymologically it means "God of wealth"[^1].

Cái (財) 'wealth, riches'; Shén (神) 'god, spirit' — the popular deity of prosperity worshipped at New Year.

The ASCII form *caishen* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Cáishén** recovers the stress accent of the original directly in the address bar. The restoration preserves at least one distinctive feature — a diacritic or a distinctive letter — that the ASCII form loses, and exactly one historically valid Unicode restoration exists, which places the name in Tier 1.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **c** → **C** — Same, capitalized
- **a** → **á** — Acute tone mark
- **i** → **i** — Same
- **s** → **s** — Same
- **h** → **h** — Same
- **e** → **é** — Acute tone mark
- **n** → **n** — Same

The canonical temple for this name is served at **caishen.com**[^2].

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/caishen/** — Chinese Reconstruction.[^1]

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **C** — Initial character of the restored form Cáishén.
- **áishén** — Remainder of the name, preserving the distinctive marks of the Chinese tradition.

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: 'CAISHEN' — pronounce the restored form with attention to the preserved diacritics and length.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Chinese** — Cáishén, the restored Unicode form of the name

Cáishén is Tier 1 because the Chinese form preserves distinctive features that ASCII loses: stress, length, or special characters.

sections.body: The name is written in Chinese characters as **財神**. This original script is the form against which the ASCII fallback *caishen* and the PuniCodex restoration **Cáishén** are measured: the restoration preserves its pitch accent of the written form, so that a reader typing the modern address still speaks the ancient name.[^1]

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
The stories of **Cáishén** circulate within the Chinese corpus, where the figure embodies wealth, prosperity, new year.[^1]

### Primary Attestation (Sources)

Cáishén is attested in the canonical Chinese sources as a figure associated with wealth, prosperity, new year.[^1]

### Name and Meaning (Etymology)

The name means "God of wealth" and reflects the figure's role in the tradition. **Cáishén** is the Chinese god of wealth, appearing in several forms including Zhào Gōngmíng, Bǐ Gān, and Fàn Lí. He confers prosperity on families and businesses during the Lunar New Year, when images of him are displayed and burned as offerings.[^1] His cult reflects the moral ambiguity of wealth: it must be attracted ethically and shared generously. Merchants place his image beside cash registers and householders burn paper effigies to ensure his favor in the coming year.[^1]

sections.label: Syncretism & Reception
sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
Cáishén appears within the Chinese tradition and has influenced later retellings, artistic depictions, and scholarly study. The Unicode restoration preserves the name's distinctive orthography for contemporary use.[^1]

Within the Chinese tradition, closely related names in the corpus include [[bagua|Bāguà]], [[change|Cháng'é]], [[fuxi|Fúxī]], [[guandi|Guāndì]], [[guanyin|Guānyīn]], and [[houyi|Hòuyì]].

sections.label: Cultural Legacy
sections.purpose: Modern influence, literature, art, popular culture, and contemporary practice.
sections.body: Cáishén continues to appear in scholarship, art, and popular reception as a significant figure of the Chinese tradition. Restoring the name in Unicode returns the original marks that ASCII removes.[^1] Cáishén remains one of the most commonly invoked deities in Chinese popular religion, especially during New Year observances.[^1]

sections.label: Classical Texts
sections.body:
Cáishén has no canonical pre-Qin text; he is a product of **Chinese vernacular religion** and **Ming-Qing novels** such as the **Fēngshén Yǎnyì**, which dramatises the apotheosis of Zhao Gongming as god of wealth.[^1] Local gazetteers and New Year customs supply the liturgical framework.[^2]

The god's late textual formation reflects the market economy and urban temple culture of late imperial China.

sources.citation: Chinese folk religion (regional cults and underworld traditions).

sections.editorNotes: Synthesized from canonical sources by PuniCodex Team.

sections.label: Daoist Sources
sections.body:
The **Dàozàng** includes ritual manuals for inviting Cáishén during New Year and business openings, often identifying him with the martial deity **Zhào Gōngmíng** and his black tiger.[^1] Daoist wealth talismans bearing the title Cáishén circulate widely in popular practice.[^2]

The god is therefore as much a Daoist ritual creation as a folk deity.

sources.citation: Daoist Canon (Daozang), ritual manuals for wealth deities.

sections.editorNotes: Synthesized from canonical sources by PuniCodex Team.

sections.label: Buddhist Sources
sections.body:
Chinese Buddhism contributed the **Treasure-Producing Buddha** (*Nánsǎicái Fó*) and the **Yellow God of Wealth** (*Huáng Cáishén*) to the Cáishén complex.[^1] Mahāyāna sutras on merit and prosperity were recited alongside folk invocations during the New Year.[^2]

The Buddhist strand emphasises that wealth is a karmic reward compatible with moral conduct.

sources.citation: Chinese folk religion (New Year and business rituals).

sections.label: Calligraphy & Script
sections.body:
During New Year, **財神到** (Cáishén arrives) and related couplets are written in lucky red ink, often in florid **xíngshū** (running script).[^1] The characters **財神** themselves combine the radical for "shell/money" (貝) with the graph for "spirit," making the name a miniature icon of prosperity.[^2]

The restoration **Cáishén** preserves the second-tone rise that announces the god's arrival.

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body: Cáishén embodies wealth, prosperity, new year in the Chinese imagination. The name's restoration is not merely cosmetic: it recovers the stress, length, and script that make the figure recognizable in the source tradition.[^1]
